voice: A light crosses the seabed, and the shape of a wooden ship emerges from darkness. After centuries underwater, why have parts of its hull survived when so much wood usually disappears?
visual: ROV-lit oblique view of an illustrative ancient wooden merchant wreck on deep Black Sea seabed, modest surviving hull and rigging remnants, slow approach from darkness.

voice: The answer begins around the ship rather than inside it. Water above the wreck is arranged in layers, and those layers help determine which processes can attack the surviving timber.
visual: ROV-lit close tracking along weathered hull planking into surrounding dark water, no fish or sunlight, restrained stable camera.

voice: But one correction belongs at the beginning: the Black Sea is not an empty, lifeless ocean. Its oxygenated upper waters and its oxygen-free depths are very different environments within one basin.
visual: Sunlit oxygenated Black Sea upper water with a modest small group of fish near natural rocky coast, restrained wide underwater drift, no wreck.

voice: Even the deep water is not sterile. Microorganisms can live through chemical pathways that do not require oxygen, so exceptional preservation does not mean that every biological process has simply stopped.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual microscopic cells in a dark-water explanatory background, modest abstract shapes, no actual species identification or giant glowing organisms on wood.

voice: We will follow the evidence from a hull to the water column, then return to the ship with a more precise understanding of what survives, what changes, and what remains uncertain.
visual: ROV-lit wide side view of a modest wooden wreck footprint with surviving hull sides and partly buried lower timbers, slow lateral glide.

voice: Our setting is the Black Sea, linked to the Mediterranean through narrow waterways. Rivers supply comparatively fresh water, while more saline water entering below helps establish a strong difference in density.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual regional terrain-and-water view of the Black Sea and its narrow southern connection, no exact surveyed map, slow elevated drift.

voice: That geography matters because a shipwreck does not preserve itself. Its fate depends on the environment it enters, the damage it brings down, and the disturbances that reach it after sinking.
visual: Illustrative Classical-period merchant ship on a calm Black Sea coast, conservative wooden hull and square sail, empty distant deck, slow exterior side tracking.

voice: A wreck can therefore become both an archaeological object and an environmental record. Reading it well means keeping the original vessel, the sinking event, and later changes distinct throughout the investigation.
visual: ROV-lit oblique close view of a broken hull edge meeting undisturbed seabed, restrained focus shift between timber and surrounding sediment.

voice: We are not reconstructing a witnessed final voyage. Historical scenes illustrate plausible work and materials, while the submerged images explain archaeological relationships without claiming that every detail belongs to one known wreck.
visual: Illustrative Classical-period shipyard on open Black Sea shore, one mature adult shipwright aged fifty examining timber, plain tunic, slow exterior medium tracking.

voice: The opening question is simple enough to hold in mind: what is different about the place where this wood came to rest, and how much of its survival can that difference explain?
visual: ROV exterior approaching a modest deep wooden wreck at respectful distance, lamps illuminate hull without contact or sediment disturbance, slow stable move.

voice: Begin with the ship as a built object. A wooden hull consists of shaped pieces and connections, whose arrangement can record decisions about construction, repair, maintenance, and the work of seafaring.
visual: Illustrative Classical-period shipbuilding close-up of mature hands fitting a shaped plank beside a wooden hull on firm open shore, no exact ship-type claim.

voice: A surviving joint can be more informative than a general silhouette. Its location and relationship to neighboring timbers may help distinguish original construction from later repair, provided the evidence is recorded carefully.
visual: ROV-lit macro of an ordinary wooden hull connection and adjacent planks, no invented diagnostic inscription or numbered tags, slow side slider.

voice: A mast or steering component can also preserve a relationship that a scattered cargo alone cannot show. The value lies in connected parts, not merely in the spectacle of an old object.
visual: ROV-lit medium view of an illustrative surviving low mast element and hull-side steering timber, no intact raised sail, slow oblique camera.

voice: That is why some Black Sea discoveries have drawn unusual attention. Their preservation allows questions about ships as structures, rather than forcing every reconstruction to begin with a few isolated fragments.
visual: ROV-lit wide oblique view of connected ancient hull timbers with modest upright elements, natural dark water and sparse suspended particles, slow pullback.

voice: In twenty eighteen, the Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project publicized a remarkably preserved Classical-period trading ship, dated approximately to the fourth century before our era, lying more than two kilometers deep.
visual: ROV-lit illustrative Classical merchant wreck with surviving hull and limited mast remnants on deep seabed, no exact named-site geometry or claimed discovery footage.

voice: The announcement gave a concrete example of what the deep environment can retain. It did not establish that every Black Sea wreck survives equally well, or that all surviving timber remains physically sound.
visual: ROV-lit close view of a preserved-looking but weathered hull plank edge, subtle irregular surface, slow steady tracking, no strength test.

voice: Dating also needs a subject. A dated timber sample helps constrain the age of the wood; interpreting construction and loss still requires context, possible reuse, and the other evidence from the wreck.
visual: ROV-lit macro of a single attached weathered timber within its hull context, no sampling, cutting or loose artifact removal, slow focus shift.

voice: Likewise, a modern label describing a ship as intact is relative. It can emphasize extraordinary structural survival without meaning every original fitting, surface, cargo item, and voyage record has remained complete.
visual: ROV-lit wide view showing connected hull sides alongside plainly missing upper structures and partly buried portions, slow lateral glide.

voice: Before looking for a chemical explanation, notice that range of survival. Some features remain exposed, some may lie beneath sediment, and others were damaged before the vessel ever reached the bottom.
visual: ROV-lit tracking from exposed hull planking toward an undisturbed sediment-covered lower edge, no magical reveal or excavation.

voice: The first answer is therefore architectural: we are studying an assemblage with a history. The environmental answer becomes useful when it explains why particular parts of that assemblage escaped particular forms of destruction.
visual: ROV-lit side view of a wooden hull section with several connected timbers and a broken margin, quiet restrained camera, no people.

voice: Wood at sea normally faces several kinds of loss. Organisms can consume or weaken it, physical forces can break and scatter it, and burial or exposure can change the conditions around it.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual wooden hull section in a generic marine setting with separate intact, worn and sediment-covered areas, explanatory scale, no real-site diagnosis.

voice: Large marine wood borers can rapidly remove material where conditions allow them to thrive. Their activity is one reason a familiar wooden hull may disappear while heavier cargo survives on the seabed.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual close-up of wood with small abstract boring channels in a generic oxygenated marine setting, no giant monster worms or exact specimen claim.

voice: The creatures commonly called shipworms are actually boring bivalves, not ordinary worms. Their name is memorable, but their biology and environmental requirements are more useful than a frightening picture of their appearance.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual small wood-boring bivalve form beside a simplified wood channel, neutral explanatory background, no photoreal unverified species identity.

voice: Oxygen availability is important for many such animals. Remove suitable oxygenated conditions and you can restrict important agents of attack, changing what remains possible for the wood around a particular wreck site.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual comparison of a generic wood surface in oxygenated water and a separate low-oxygen case, no measured decay rate or universal threshold.

voice: That does not make oxygen the only control. Temperature, salinity, sediment cover, wood properties, exposure history, and physical disturbance can all influence the condition of archaeological timber in different marine environments.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual hull timber meeting water and seabed sediment, restrained diagrammatic textures over a dark outdoor marine background, no data labels.

voice: Nor does the absence of large borers prove that no decay remains. Microbial processes can continue under conditions that exclude many animals, and visually recognizable wood can still have changed within its structure.
visual: ROV-lit close-up of recognizably shaped but weathered timber with ordinary surface irregularities, no invented visible microbial colony, slow slider.

voice: Preservation is therefore selective. One process may be strongly limited while another continues more slowly, and the resulting object can retain its shape without preserving every original material property or biological component.
visual: ROV-lit macro of an incomplete plank edge and surviving adjoining hull connection, no testing or flexing, gentle oblique camera.

voice: This distinction matters whenever a camera makes an old hull look ready to sail. Appearance can reveal useful geometry, but appearance alone cannot establish strength, flexibility, chemical stability, or readiness for recovery.
visual: ROV-lit wide side view of a recognizably shaped ancient hull with missing pieces, slow stable pullback, no restoration or sailing transformation.

voice: To understand the difference, we need to move upward through the water. The same sea can place one ship in an oxygenated environment and another beneath a very different chemical regime.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual water-column cutaway with a shallow wreck location and a separate deep wreck location, no exact depth boundary, slow vertical camera.

voice: Depth will help locate those environments, but it is not itself the mechanism. The relevant questions concern density, water exchange, oxygen supply and consumption, and the conditions actually present around the wreck.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual water column with broad gradual density and oxygen shading, no sharp physical wall or measured profile, slow vertical drift.

voice: Water is not always mixed evenly from surface to bottom. When layers differ strongly in density, vertical exchange becomes more difficult, allowing very different chemical conditions to persist within the same basin.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual cross-section of layered basin water, restrained overlapping blue-gray gradients rather than solid partitions, open-sea backdrop.

voice: In the Black Sea, comparatively fresh river water contributes to a less saline upper layer. More saline water entering through the southern connection contributes to denser water below, helping maintain the stratification.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual river-to-basin section with a fresher upper inflow and separate denser lower inflow, clear restrained geometry, no exact currents map.

voice: Temperature also affects density, and circulation remains more complicated than two perfectly uniform tanks. Our simple section explains the main relationship without pretending to reproduce every seasonal or regional variation in the sea.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual layered water column with soft varying bands and gentle lateral variation, no two rigid tanks or precisely labeled temperatures.

voice: At the surface, contact with the atmosphere and biological production help supply oxygen. Mixing can distribute it through upper waters, supporting communities very different from those living farther down the water column.
visual: Sunlit oxygenated upper Black Sea water near rocky coast with modest fish and suspended natural plankton-like particles, slow restrained drift.

voice: Organic material produced above can sink. As microorganisms and other processes break it down, dissolved oxygen is consumed, so maintaining oxygen at depth requires a continuing supply rather than a one-time gift.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual small organic particles sinking through a water column, natural darkening gradient, no glowing debris or measured oxygen values.

voice: If the supply is restricted while consumption continues, deeper water can lose its oxygen. That balance between delivery and use is more explanatory than simply calling the whole sea dark, salty, or motionless.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual basin section with limited vertical exchange indicated only by restrained abstract motion, dark deep zone, no closed lid or exact flow arrows.

voice: The Black Sea's deep basin contains a large body of persistently anoxic water. Anoxic means without dissolved oxygen under the conditions being described; it does not mean the water contains no chemical activity.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual deep basin water below a lighter upper band, no fish, no literal colored barrier, steady exterior-section view.

voice: The deep water is also commonly described as euxinic, meaning oxygen-free and containing sulfide. Those terms are related but not identical, and we should not apply them carelessly to every layer we encounter.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual water column distinguishing a broad oxygenated upper zone, transition and deep sulfidic zone through soft shading, no readable labels.

voice: Between the upper and deep environments lies a transition with its own chemistry. Its position and thickness can vary, so a convenient single depth should not become an unchanging boundary across the entire sea.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual basin section with gently varying transition depth across the frame, no universal numerical boundary or sharp glass-like interface.

voice: That is the second major answer: the Black Sea is vertically differentiated. To explain a wreck, locate its setting within that structure rather than assigning every part of the basin one environmental label.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual wide Black Sea water-column view with a modest wreck silhouette deep below the upper zone, restrained slow pullback.

voice: Now place a wooden hull in the deeper oxygen-free environment. Important oxygen-dependent wood-boring animals cannot operate there as they would in suitable oxygenated water, removing one major route by which timber can disappear.
visual: ROV-lit close tracking along connected deep hull planks, clear ordinary wood grain and modest sediment, no borers or visible fish.

voice: The result can be remarkable survival of structural elements, including parts that are rarely found together in more destructive settings. Connected wood can preserve evidence about construction and use that scattered artifacts cannot replace.
visual: ROV-lit oblique view of connected hull, deck-edge remnants and limited steering elements, modest ancient merchant scale, slow lateral movement.

voice: But notice the wording: one major route of destruction is restricted. It would be a mistake to turn that into a claim that the wreck has been completely sterilized or made permanently immune to change.
visual: ROV-lit macro of irregular weathered planking and a partly broken joint, quiet deep water, no pristine polished timber.

voice: The chemistry does not erase the ship's earlier history. Damage during a collision, storm, fire, grounding, or descent would need its own evidence, and missing material may predate contact with the seabed.
visual: ROV-lit view of a broken bow-side timber in an illustrative wreck, no reenacted cause, no flames, collision or storm asserted.

voice: Nor does a protective setting guarantee that the hull arrived gently. The configuration on the bottom may combine the vessel's original architecture with collapse, impact, sediment movement, and later disturbance at the wreck site.
visual: ROV-lit wide view of a modest tilted hull with some displaced timber nearby, undisturbed sediment, no dynamic sinking or impact scene.

voice: An exceptional wreck therefore needs two explanations: why enough material survived to study, and how the surviving arrangement came to take its present form. The first does not automatically solve the second question.
visual: ROV-lit slow overhead oblique pass across hull sides and adjacent scattered pieces, no excavating or touching, stable camera.

voice: That is also why different materials must be assessed separately. Timber, rope, metal, ceramics, and other remains respond differently to the surrounding chemistry and to changes in burial, exposure, and physical handling over time.
visual: ROV-lit illustrative hull section with attached rope remnants and plain amphora-like ceramic forms partly embedded in sediment, no treasure or artifact removal.

voice: A ceramic vessel surviving beside a hull does not prove that every organic item aboard survived equally. An impressive photograph can contain several materials with different preservation histories within a very small area.
visual: ROV-lit close view of weathered timber beside a plain partially buried ceramic container, slow focus shift, no readable decoration or contents claim.

voice: The useful question is therefore specific: which feature survived, what condition is it in, and which environmental or physical processes best account for it at this particular location and point in its history?
visual: ROV-lit macro-to-medium tracking along one attached hull connection within wider wreck context, no measured condition map, steady motion.

voice: We can answer that without claiming to know every detail. A mechanism becomes stronger when it explains a pattern across evidence, rather than relying only on the most spectacular-looking ship in the collection.
visual: ROV-lit wide side view of a modest ancient hull against dark seabed, slow pullback, no giant ship or sensational glowing outline.

voice: The third part of the answer concerns life. In the upper Black Sea, oxygenated water supports familiar marine organisms and productive communities. Nothing about a deep anoxic layer makes those upper waters universally lifeless.
visual: Sunlit upper Black Sea water with a modest fish group over natural rocky substrate, slow wide lateral drift, no deep wreck.

voice: Farther down, microorganisms can use different chemical pathways. Researchers have identified distinct microbial communities across oxygenated, transitional, and sulfidic layers, demonstrating that the biological story changes with the water column rather than simply ending.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual microscopic community forms arranged beside a soft water-column gradient, no actual species portraits or measured abundances, explanatory scene.

voice: Some microbial activity helps transform carbon and sulfur compounds under oxygen-poor conditions. That activity belongs to the ecosystem and can influence the environment in which archaeological material survives, even when large animals are absent.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual small particles and microbial forms in a deep-water explanatory backdrop, restrained abstract interactions, no actual chemical formula or site sample claim.

voice: We do not need to imagine visible clouds of giant bacteria covering every hull. Much of this activity occurs at scales and through measurements that ordinary archaeological video does not directly reveal to viewers.
visual: ROV-lit ordinary dark hull surface at natural camera scale, no glowing colonies or oversized microscopic organisms, slow slider.

voice: A camera may show the absence of visible fish around a particular deep wreck, but that image alone cannot identify every microbial process or establish the chemical profile of the surrounding water at all times.
visual: ROV-lit wide wreck view in deep dark water without fish, no sensors or numerical overlay, stable slow drift.

voice: The same discipline applies above. A lively surface scene does not tell us the oxygen concentration at a distant seabed site. The two observations concern different locations within a strongly structured marine environment.
visual: Calm sunlit Black Sea surface seen from a low exterior sea-level viewpoint, no seabed visible or impossible transparent two-kilometer view.

voice: The most useful contrast is therefore between environments, not between life and complete emptiness. Oxygen availability shapes the organisms and reactions that are possible, while other forms of life continue beyond that boundary below.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual layered water column with upper fish silhouettes and separate tiny abstract microbial forms lower down, no real measurement or sharp boundary.

voice: This matters for the wood because decay is not one universal action. Different organisms and chemical conditions can affect different components at different rates, leaving an object recognizable without leaving it materially unchanged inside.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual wood section showing a recognizable outer form and modest simplified altered internal structure, not an actual microscope image or diagnostic result.

voice: A protective environment can thus preserve information while allowing change. The correct picture is selective survival within an active system, rather than an ancient ship placed inside a perfectly sealed and sterile glass display case.
visual: ROV-lit hull seen through ordinary dark water with subtle suspended particles, no glass enclosure, natural imperfect preservation, slow pullback.

voice: We have now separated two claims that are often confused: deep conditions can greatly favor preservation of some wooden remains, and the Black Sea contains multiple living environments. Both can be true together without contradiction.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual wide basin section linking a sunlit upper band and a separately illuminated deep wreck silhouette, clearly explanatory rather than actual transparent sea.

voice: What about the depth where the conditions change? Public descriptions often give a rounded figure, but real profiles vary by place, season, circulation, and the particular chemical quantity being measured in the water column.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual several adjacent water profiles with softly differing transition levels, no numbers, no actual sampled stations, restrained camera.

voice: An oxygen-poor transition is not automatically identical to the first appearance of sulfide. Treating every chemical boundary as one horizontal line would simplify away part of the very mechanism we are trying to understand.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual water column with distinct broad transition bands rather than one line, no readable oxygen or sulfide labels, stable exterior section.

voice: Density provides an important way to compare water masses because depth alone can shift with the physical structure. Even then, a real interpretation depends on the observations, references, and methods used to describe the profile.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual basin section with gently curved density bands and a small wreck marker, no measured values, slow side drift.

voice: For a particular shipwreck, the conditions near its timbers matter more than a number borrowed from another survey. Present observations should also be distinguished from the full environmental history since the ship reached the bottom.
visual: ROV-lit close view along the sediment-water contact at an ancient hull, quiet dark setting, no environmental sensor or claimed reading.

voice: Those histories can differ across the continental shelf, slope, and deep basin. A comparison needs location and context, rather than assuming that every wreck is exposed to one uniform Black Sea preservation regime everywhere.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual sea section showing a shelf, sloping margin and deep basin with separate generic wreck markers, no exact site positions or depths.

voice: Published studies of Black Sea wrecks have compared sites in different oxygen conditions and examined their surrounding environment. Such comparisons help turn a general explanation into questions that can be tested locally with appropriate evidence.
visual: Exterior ROV at respectful distance from a modest deep hull, lights directed along timbers, no contact or sediment disturbance, slow lateral shot.

voice: They also show why the best-preserved example should not become the only example. A less complete wreck can reveal how exposure, setting, or disturbance changed the losses and survivals at another archaeological site.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual comparison of two generic wreck footprints with different degrees of surviving timber, separate explanatory panels, no actual named-site equivalence.

voice: The aim is not to rank wrecks by beauty. It is to understand which differences in material, history, and environment explain the pattern, and where alternative explanations still need to be kept open for investigation.
visual: ROV-lit partial wooden hull with plainly missing upper portions, modest unglamorous preservation, slow steady pullback, no treasure.

voice: A useful environmental model can therefore become more complicated as evidence improves. Regional stratification remains important, while local circulation, sediment cover, and the condition of the vessel refine what we expect to find at each site.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual deep wreck at a seabed margin with modest sediment cover and broad water layers above, no precise circulation map.

voice: That is a stronger story than a magical depth below which everything survives forever. It explains why some discoveries are exceptional while leaving room for variation, continuing decay, and the physical risks that remain around them.
visual: ROV-lit wide view of a partly preserved ancient wooden wreck, ordinary missing elements visible, dark water, no magical barrier or preserved-for-ever lettering.

voice: At great depth, remotely operated vehicles bring lights and cameras beyond ordinary human diving. Their connection to a surface support system allows controlled observation without placing divers beside the wreck.
visual: Exterior modern ROV descending through dark open Black Sea water with tether and lamps, no human diver, slow stable follow shot.

voice: Black Sea MAP used robotic surveys to study deep archaeological remains. Their equipment made it possible to record connected structures that had previously been difficult to examine directly in place.
visual: Exterior ROV holding station near a wooden wreck and illuminating a modest hull area, no exact named vehicle logo or claimed expedition footage.

voice: The lighting matters. More than two kilometers down, a sunlit turquoise wreck would misrepresent the environment. Artificial lamps reveal part of a hull within darkness, rather than illuminating an entire sea.
visual: ROV lamps reveal weathered hull planks surrounded by near-black water, realistic falloff and limited visibility, slow oblique camera, no sunlight.

voice: Fish weaving through that deep anoxic hull would also give the wrong impression. The upper sea supports familiar animals; they should not be moved into another environment merely as decoration.
visual: ROV-lit deep hull without fish or divers, sparse ordinary particles, restrained camera, no coral or seaweed garden.

voice: The vehicle needs distance and control. Movement, lighting, and perspective affect recording, while contact or disturbed sediment could damage the relationships that make the wreck archaeologically useful to future investigation.
visual: Exterior ROV at safe respectful standoff from fragile hull timber, gentle stationary posture and tether, no thruster plume touching sediment.

voice: A sharp image is not a complete investigation. Recording needs coverage, scale, and orientation, including awareness of hidden surfaces. The most dramatic camera view does not necessarily provide the fullest record.
visual: ROV-lit oblique wide wreck view with one partly obscured side and ordinary shadows, slow steady lateral pass, no measured scale overlay.

voice: A low angle can make a modest hull look monumental. That perspective cannot become a measurement of original height, capacity, age, or importance. Attention and archaeological inference remain different tasks.
visual: ROV-lit low oblique view of a modest surviving wooden hull side, no exaggerated giant scale, steady slow camera.

voice: Connect the images through a documented spatial framework. Then a dramatic perspective can be checked against relationships among the surviving parts, instead of quietly becoming the whole interpretation of the vessel.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual overhead arrangement of connected hull timbers on a dark seabed background, clearly illustrative, no exact survey grid or coordinates.

voice: Even an overview has gaps. Sediment, timbers, and unrecorded areas can hide evidence. A polished reconstruction should identify those uncertainties rather than making them disappear without explanation in the finished image.
visual: ROV-lit overhead view of a hull partly buried beneath undisturbed sediment, no x-ray reveal or clearing action, slow drift.

voice: The robot provides access, not automatic answers. Its value is the chance to record evidence carefully enough that later claims about construction, history, and preservation can be checked against actual observations.
visual: Exterior ROV lamps illuminate an attached hull connection, vehicle remains away from the timber, quiet deep-water shot, no manipulation.

voice: Overlapping photographs can support a three-dimensional model when handled correctly. Combining viewpoints helps retain relationships that one picture may hide or exaggerate. The model remains derived from observations, not an ancient blueprint.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual three-dimensional outline of a modest hull over a dark seabed background, clearly derived illustrative mesh, no software interface or exact data.

voice: Visual detail alone does not date the ship. Nor does a detailed surface automatically reveal cargo, nationality, voyage, or cause of loss. Those questions need evidence suited to each particular claim.
visual: ROV-lit macro of plain weathered timber and an ordinary hull joint, no inscription, flag or invented diagnostic cargo, slow slider.

voice: Construction details, associated objects, samples, and historical comparisons contribute different kinds of evidence. Their strengths should remain visible, rather than being merged into one confident story merely because the pictures are persuasive.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual arrangement of a hull joint, plain ceramic shape and timber fragment outline, no actual detached artifacts, dark marine explanatory backdrop.

voice: A timber may come from an older tree or have been reused. A date therefore constrains possibilities without erasing archaeological context. Dating wood and dating a ship's loss are related but separate questions.
visual: ROV-lit attached timber with natural grain and worn surface, no cutting, sample extraction or exact tree rings claimed, slow focus shift.

voice: Comparison with an ancient depiction can suggest questions about ship type. It does not prove every depicted detail. Surviving timber can independently test ideas that an image simplifies or leaves unexplained.
visual: Illustrative Classical-period wooden merchant ship at a quiet Black Sea harbor, conservative square sail and hull form, no copied ancient artwork or figurative vase imagery.

voice: That is why connected wood matters. It may preserve joints, working spaces, or component relationships that written descriptions never needed to explain. Exceptional survival can expand the questions available to archaeology.
visual: ROV-lit close view of connected hull planks, a cross-timber and modest attached rope remnant, no complete intact deck, slow lateral glide.

voice: Do not build a perfect imaginary ship by combining the best feature from every discovery. Wrecks belong to different periods, traditions, and histories, despite resting within the same large marine basin.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual separate silhouettes of modest ancient and later wooden merchant hulls, clearly distinct panels, no composite fantasy ship, neutral dark backdrop.

voice: Historical scenes illustrate tasks and materials. An adult shipwright shaping timber is not a recovered portrait, a documented repair, or the known final afternoon of the particular wreck being discussed here.
visual: Illustrative Classical-period mature adult shipwright aged fifty shaping a plank on firm open shore, conservative simple hand tool, no identified person or exact event.

voice: Keep observation, measurement, dating, and reconstruction connected but distinct. A film should show which category an image belongs to, so a useful illustration does not silently become evidence for its own details.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual paired views of solid surviving hull portions and faint proposed missing outlines, clearly differentiated explanatory layers, no actual recovered blueprint.

voice: Uncertainty can then guide investigation. It identifies observations that could strengthen an explanation, rather than allowing a compelling reconstruction to replace evidence that has not yet been recovered or properly assessed.
visual: ROV-lit wide view of a partially preserved wreck with shadowed and sediment-covered portions, quiet realistic light falloff, slow pullback.

voice: Low oxygen restricts particular biological attacks, but it cannot prevent physical damage. An object striking exposed timber can destroy relationships regardless of how long chemistry has favored the wood's survival before that moment.
visual: ROV-lit close view of exposed fragile hull timbers against dark seabed, no actual damage event, fishing gear or aggressor depicted, slow slider.

voice: Studies along parts of the Black Sea margin have compared wreck condition with oceanography and impacts such as bottom trawling. Exposure depends on location, depth, and the activities reaching each site.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual shelf-and-slope section with generic wreck locations and a separate distant vessel silhouette, no exact fishing route or current activity claim.

voice: Depth may limit access without guaranteeing protection. Ask what actually reaches a wreck, rather than assuming that conditions restricting certain organisms also prevent every other kind of disturbance or material loss there.
visual: ROV-lit wide hull at modest deep seabed slope, ordinary fragile elements visible, no fishing scene or invulnerability shield.

voice: Sediment can protect material by limiting exposure, then uncover it again as conditions change. Buried and exposed portions of the same ship may therefore experience different environments through time at that site.
visual: ROV-lit tracking along the boundary between exposed hull planks and an undisturbed sediment-covered section, no active uncovering, slow stable movement.

voice: Seabed shape matters too. A hull on a slope and timber supported by sediment have different mechanical situations. Water chemistry alone cannot describe every force acting on the surviving archaeological remains.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual side section of a modest tilted hull partly supported by soft seabed, no precise stability model, restrained dark marine background.

voice: A changed photograph needs interpretation. Visibility, lamp position, sediment cover, and actual damage can all change appearances. Comparison and context are needed before declaring measured loss or a newly exposed structural feature.
visual: ROV-lit ordinary hull edge under limited visibility and uneven lamp falloff, no before-and-after damage graphic or invented discovery, slow camera.

voice: Preservation is a continuing condition, not a permanent label awarded at discovery. Materials, exposure, and access can change, while parts of one wreck may respond differently over the same interval of time.
visual: ROV-lit wide wreck view with exposed, partly buried and shadowed timbers in one frame, dark water, slow lateral drift.

voice: Protection begins by understanding what survives and what threatens it. Discovery brings attention, but attention alone does not provide the resources, knowledge, or sustained care needed to retain archaeological information for later study.
visual: Exterior ROV holding respectful distance above a deep wreck, lamps cover a modest area, no contact, quiet restrained shot.

voice: Anoxia is not a physical fence around the hull. Biological, chemical, and mechanical conditions must be considered together when deciding how to document the material and keep its relationships available in place.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual deep hull with broad surrounding water and sediment zones, no barrier or protective bubble, restrained explanatory geometry.

voice: Should the ship simply be raised? An underwater image can make recovery look like moving a solid object. Waterlogged materials and their surrounding context make the actual decision considerably more complicated than that.
visual: Exterior sea-surface view of a modern support vessel at a distance under natural daylight, no wreck lifting or crane recovery, calm water.

voice: Waterlogged wood can keep its shape while losing strength. Recovery changes support and environment; uncontrolled drying may cause damage. Survival underwater does not guarantee stability in air.
visual: Unlabelled conceptual waterlogged timber held within its seabed context, modest internal structure shading, no actual recovery or drying demonstration, dark marine background.

voice: Conservation belongs before recovery decisions. Material, condition, context, questions, and capacity for continuing care matter. The challenge extends beyond the moment cameras record an impressive discovery.
visual: ROV-lit close view of fragile attached timber and adjacent undisturbed seabed, no handling, laboratory, scientist or recovery sling, slow focus shift.

voice: Leaving remains in place can protect information through recording and appropriate care. Raising an artifact does not automatically preserve the relationships that once surrounded it underwater.
visual: ROV-lit wide hull within its seabed context, stable quiet artificial light, no enclosure or artifact removal, slow pullback.

voice: Removal can separate an object from position, orientation, neighboring pieces, and deposits. Those relationships may explain use or loss, despite looking less impressive than the object.
visual: ROV-lit plain ceramic container partly embedded beside connected hull timbers, camera remains still before a gentle side move, no grabbing arm.

voice: Sampling answers valuable questions when purpose, location, and recording are justified. A timber sample is evidence, rather than a souvenir collected because the robot can reach it.
visual: ROV exterior facing an attached hull plank without touching, no sampling tool action, respectful standoff, quiet dark-water lamps.

voice: Recording a joint may retain relationships that disturbance would erase. Dramatic intervention is not necessarily most informative, especially when future methods could ask better questions of preserved material.
visual: ROV-lit macro of an intact-looking hull connection left in place, light falls gently across wood grain, no manipulation, slow slider.

voice: Evidence has disappeared or remains hidden. Attempts to make everything visible can themselves damage context. The ship is therefore not an untouched container waiting to surrender all its history.
visual: ROV-lit partially buried hull side and shadowed lower timbers, undisturbed sediment, no clearing plume or exposed complete interior.

voice: Ask which observation improves understanding while retaining context. Interpretation can explain that practical choice without turning the wreck into either a recovery spectacle or a catalog of warnings.
visual: Exterior ROV making a slow noncontact pass parallel to a modest hull side, no human operators or room, stable lamps and tether.

voice: The value is connected material, not merely old wood. Its relationships can reveal technology, people, and environments that isolated objects or descriptions would make harder to investigate.
visual: ROV-lit wide view of connected hull timbers and a few plain ceramic forms in context, no treasure, slow outward drift.

voice: A hull can reveal construction choices and working relationships. It does not automatically explain a whole community, its trading network, or the experiences of everyone who traveled aboard.
